title: Donald Hebb and "Neurons That Fire Together, Wire Together" (1949)
explainer: In his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior, psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that a connection between two neurons strengthens when one repeatedly helps drive the other to fire - the biological rule now shorthanded as 'neurons that fire together, wire together.' This postulate, decades before anyone trained a deep network, is the direct ancestor of how we think about learned weights as distributed, associative representations rather than lookup tables - which is precisely the intuition mechanistic interpretability work tries to recover when it goes hunting for 'circuits' and features inside a trained model. It's a useful reminder that the idea of understanding a network by tracing which units 'wire together' is older than computing itself.

title: John Searle's Chinese Room Argument (1980)
explainer: In 1980, philosopher John Searle proposed a thought experiment: a person alone in a room, manually following an English rulebook to manipulate Chinese symbols, can produce fluent Chinese replies without understanding a word of Chinese. Searle used this to argue that manipulating symbols by syntax alone (which is all a program does) never by itself produces genuine semantic understanding - a question that sits directly underneath alignment debates about whether an interpretable 'feature' or 'circuit' found inside a model reflects real understanding or just a convincing pattern-matcher. It's a 45-year-old argument, but it's the clearest statement of the understanding-versus-simulation question that mechanistic interpretability keeps running into empirically.
